title: Your younger self

cards: An old notebook turns up in a box during a move. The handwriting is yours, but the person writing isn't quite. There's the plan to marry someone who turned out to be a disaster.
There's the cruel joke about a friend. There's the decision that cost a job, or a year, or a relationship. Some people laugh at their old notebooks; some close them fast.
Earlier this block was about forgiving yourself in general. Today is narrower: the younger one, who had less to work with. Two lines from the Bible can be read as speaking to that person.

teach.h: A CHILD UNDERSTANDS AS A CHILD.
teach.b: First, a stage, not a verdict. Paul, writing to the church at Corinth, says: "When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things."
He doesn't say the child was wicked. He says the child understood as a child. The younger self had a smaller map, and acted inside it.

teach.h: REMEMBER NOT THE SINS. REMEMBER ME.
teach.b: Psalm twenty-five asks: "Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions: according to thy mercy remember thou me for thy goodness' sake, O LORD." Two rememberings: don't remember the sins; do remember me.
The psalmist isn't asking to be excused. He's asking to be seen as more than the worst of his younger days.
Third, the trick of hindsight. Looking back, the warning signs are obvious, because now you know how it ended. Your younger self didn't.
Blaming them for not knowing the ending is like shouting at a character in a movie you've already seen. Fourth, what the line is not. I didn't know then isn't the same as it didn't matter.
If someone was hurt, amends still apply: make it right where you can.
Forgiving your younger self doesn't cancel the repair. It sets down the blame, so the person you are now has the energy to do the repairing.

how: Jews and Christians pray the Psalms, including Psalm 25 with its request not to remember the sins of youth; Christians read Paul's line about childish things as part of his chapter on love, 1 Corinthians 13.

o: the city whose church Paul told of putting away childish things
the town where Paul was born and grew up as a child
the church Paul founded in Rome for young believers

games.q: two lines about growing up — tap the pairs.
p: remember not the sins of my youth
seen as more than the worst

s: Paul calls the child he was wicked
he says he spoke, understood and thought as a child, then put childish things away.
Psalm 25 asks God to forget the sins of youth but remember the person
"remember not the sins of my youth… remember thou me."
forgiving your younger self cancels any need for amends
it stops the punishing; the repairing can go on.

games.q: you're the psalmist, thinking about what you did when you were young. what do you ask for?
o: that it be excused because you were young.
that the sins be forgotten and you be remembered.
that you never be reminded of it again.
games.why: Psalm 25 uses remember twice: remember not the sins, and remember thou me, by mercy.

practice: Bring to mind a younger you, at a particular age, in a particular room: the clothes, the hair, the phone or the lack of one.
Recall one thing that version of you did that still stings, then look at the person instead of the mistake: what did they know, what were they afraid of, who was teaching them?
If it feels right, say your line silently to them, and if you pray, hold that younger self in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Corinth. The church Paul wrote to, saying when he was a child he understood as a child, before he put away childish things. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: I didn't know then. Hindsight knows the ending; they didn't. Day nine hundred eighty-nine, done.
